example.text: こんにちは、はじめまして。

teach.meaning: こんにちは is used from late morning to early evening. In the morning, people say おはよう or おはようございます instead.
teach.sound: The last は is said “wa”, not “ha”: kon-ni-chi-wa. It's a leftover from old spelling.

blank.tip: はじめまして means “nice to meet you”, and it follows a greeting when you meet someone for the first time.

teach.meaning: ありがとう is casual, for friends and family. With teachers or strangers, say ありがとうございます.
teach.sound: The う after ご stretches the o: a-ri-ga-tō, not a-ri-ga-to-u.

blank.tip: どうも means “very much” and usually comes right before words of thanks, like ありがとう.

teach.meaning: {水|みず} means cold or room-temperature water. Hot water has its own word: おゆ.
teach.sound: Two short beats: mi-zu. The u at the end is soft and quick.

blank.tip: を comes right after the thing you're asking for, so the blank needs a noun: a thing, like water.

teach.meaning: おはよう is for family and friends. To be polite, say おはようございます.
teach.sound: The う makes the o long: o-ha-yō. Hold the last o for an extra beat.

example.text: すみません、トイレはどこですか。
example.romanization: Sumimasen, toire wa doko desu ka.
example.translation: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

teach.meaning: すみません means both “excuse me” and “sorry”. It's also the polite way to call a waiter in a restaurant.
teach.sound: The first u is very light, so it can sound like “smi-ma-sen”. The ん at the end is a full beat.

blank.tip: Before asking a stranger a question, Japanese speakers start with すみません to get their attention.

teach.meaning: はい also means “I'm here” when a teacher calls your name, and “OK” when you agree to do something.
teach.sound: One quick syllable, like the English word “hi”.

blank.tip: そうです means “that's right”, so the word before it has to be a “yes”.

teach.meaning: いいえ can sound quite direct. It's also a polite reply when someone thanks you, like “not at all”.
teach.sound: Three beats: i-i-e. Don't shorten it to いえ (ie), which means “house”.

blank.tip: ちがいます means “that's not right”, so the word before it has to be a “no”.

teach.meaning: Japanese nouns have no plural form, so ねこ can mean “a cat” or “cats”.
teach.sound: Each kana is one beat of the same length: ne-ko.

blank.tip: が marks the thing you like, so the blank needs a noun: a thing, animal or person. Describing words like {大|おお}きい need a noun after them.

example.translation: We have a dog at home.

teach.meaning: いぬ is the everyday word. Small children often say わんわん, like “woof woof”.
teach.sound: Two short beats: i-nu. Keep the u short and relaxed.

blank.tip: います is used for living things like people and animals. For objects, Japanese uses あります.

example.text: この{本|ほん}はおもしろいです。

teach.meaning: {本|ほん} also appears in {日本|にほん}, the name of Japan, where it means “origin”.
teach.sound: Two beats: ho-n. In Japanese, ん counts as a full beat on its own.

blank.tip: この means “this” and must be followed by a noun, a thing like a book.

example.text: {友|とも}だちと{話|はな}します。

teach.meaning: {友|とも}だち is also written {友達|ともだち}. The だち part once made it plural, but today it means one friend or many.
teach.sound: Four even beats: to-mo-da-chi. ち sounds like “chee”.

blank.tip: と here means “with”, and {話|はな}します means “talk”, so the blank is a person you can talk with.

teach.meaning: {食|た}べる is the dictionary form. In polite speech it becomes {食|た}べます, as in the example sentence.
teach.sound: Three even beats: ta-be-ru. The Japanese r is a light tap, somewhere between r, l and d.

example.translation: That's a big dog, isn't it?

teach.meaning: Describing words ending in い go right before the noun, like {大|おお}きいいぬ, “a big dog”. The opposite is {小|ちい}さい, “small”.
teach.sound: Four beats: o-o-ki-i. Both the o and the i are long.

blank.tip: The blank describes the dog, so it needs a describing word (an adjective), like “big”. Two nouns can't sit side by side like this.
